items.body: Nagoya’s leftfield electronic scene has recently garnered interest from the international music press. This is chiefly thanks to the efforts of producer and all-around scenester Yuya Abe (abentis). abentis has been an associate of Facta & K-LONE’s Wisdom Teeth label since 2021. After a chance encounter with Facta on the platform formerly known as Twitter, Wisdom Teeth featured abentis’ track “Bicycle” in their 2022 compilation To Illustrate. Earlier this year, abentis curated a compilation of Nagoya talent for Wisdom Teeth titled nagoyaka na kaze / 和やかな風 (quiet wind). Entries oscillate from woodblock percussion-fronted minimal house to rootsical UK bass. Now the artist returns with his debut album Dim Grow, the first physical release on his fledgling 2++ label, which he plans to use to promote the Nagoya scene. Dim Grow is fairly short, clocking in at just 41 minutes, but contains enough unique ideas to fill a longer work. “Separate” opens the album with an unhurried cavalcade of brassy splashes and arpeggiation evoking Italian experimentalist Caterina Barbieri. It segues into “In Memories,” the longest piece on Dim Grow at just over nine minutes. It’s maybe too long; physically modeled kalimba dominates the first 90 seconds until the rising tedium is suddenly leavened with bass. A Steve Reich influence looms large for the remaining seven-plus minutes, a twinkling tropical variation on the American minimalist composer’s studied drift between melodic and rhythmic phrases. Especially compelling are the reverberant marimba stabs near the end with a series of showy decay accents—essentially the audio equivalent of crisp serifs. “Far Enough” and “Lune,” channel some of abentis’ Japanese influences, particularly goopy analog synth leads reminiscent of Thousand Knives-era Ryuichi Sakamoto and Haruomi Hosono’s late 70s prog-psych experiments—albums like Cochin Moon and Paraiso that détourned western exotica-kitsch. “Far Enough” is particularly mischievous; one motif is teasing a trap-style snare line only to collapse it into a wash of static. Forays into dance music shade the second half of Dim Grow. The swung 4/4 of “Lune” could earn it a place in a more open-minded house or techno set. “Eachpath” susurrates with the restlessness of 2010s deconstructed club artists like Jam City and Lee Gamble, but grounded in the rhythmic and harmonic grooves of 90s intelligent techno acts like B12, Ken Ishii, and LA Synthesis. “Circulation” is the shortest track on the album and may also be the most dance-oriented: bedroom techno with dubby mallet percussion running in opposite directions over male voices that lie on the threshold of discernibility. It’s easy to envision this music issuing from the soundsystem of a chic Nagoya(ka) sake bar, and if abentis gets his way, audiophile venues the world over. (Marcello Ursic)

items.body: Review by Steve Conrad — An Apocalyptic COVID-Confectionary ConstructionApocalyptic: "Relating to or predicting widespread destruction or the collapse of civilization." (American Heritage Dictionary of the English Language).I mean, look at this cover art- it positions the Rock Boutique as the last outpost of...something...before one ventures into the apocalyptic wilderness- the Elon Musk-esque rocket ship preparing to exit the planet (whichever planet this may be), the more-angular St. Louis arch, the slightly blood-shot mechanical eye in full surveillance mode, and the almost confectionary-appearing glowing purple...objects, which are (menacingly?) beginning to multiply within Morri's domain.And the "wheel in the sky"- biblical Ezekiel reference- and yes, what the heck is that reference? While the stream (with fiery twinkles) wends its way through the landscape.The COVID-ConfectionSo, on this third album from Chicago, USA's "progressive rock collective, REFESTRAMUS, the stage is set for the seven (on Bandcamp, nine) tracks featured on "Morri's Rock Boutique).I'm hearing these tracks- whichever version of the album you choose- as "COVID-Confection" since according to the band's bio- drummer/songwriter/lyricist Derek Ferguson formed the first incarnation of REFESTRAMUS during the initial onslaught of the worldwide global scourge of COVID, and the music on this album at least for me- an early progressive rock geek- reeks of the sort of touches that made Styx a lot of money, as well as the grandeur and flourishes that endeared many of us folks-of-a-certain-age to the progressive genre.I remember a faintly condescending review (probably in Rolling Stone, which in those days was holy writ for me) of one of the 70's era KANSAS albums, in which the all-knowing reviewer said something like, "it's fairly decent music, but with wedding-cake arrangements". Little did this reviewer know that these "wedding cake" arrangements were exactly what made some of us geeks sit up and pay attention!Which is to say that on this album, where are many "confectionary" sections that delight an aging geek, and might delight you as well, regardless of your age and geekiness. Keyboardist/vocalist Dyanne Potter Vogetlin provides standout synth and keyboard fills and flourishes that genuinely soar, that color the overall sound with richness and verve. One can hear this almost from the very beginning of the album.To this reviewer, the bass guitar and vocal prowess of Jan Christiana are almost other-worldly. Upon first hearing, I wondered who on earth could actually sing that high, with that kind of power and control? Well, Jan can. I suspect Jan also has a lot to do with the vocal arrangements, which are lush and varied, and become an additional "unsung" instrument in the confectionary construction of "Morri's Rock Boutique".So yes, even on the opening "Storms" and then certainly on the (Russian folk tale-based) "The Cossack's Dream", we get the kind of grandeur and sweep of early era progressive and glam-rock music. I had to think of AVIARY and of course Styx, sometimes even Queen due to the vocal flourishes.None of this is to diminish or minimize the contributions of each musician- it is a "rock collective" of accomplished musicians who play supremely well together, and given a spacious production by Ian Beaubout. The variety of approaches on this album is also worth mentioning, including the Russian, and later the Asian touches complete with instrumentation like shamisen, koto, and shakuhachi found on "Lakeview Samurai"- engagingly sung by Nam Chumo.Lakeview Samurai appeals to me like confection- surface sweetness, not so much substance. I can get the references to some of the current cultural scene, and the side-by-side transposition of the ancient and venerable samurai code. Everything is done well, it simply doesn't touch me very deeply, nor perhaps, fit within the framework of this album.Same goes for "Hell or NYC", pointing out the stereotypes (and perhaps well-deserved) of the coldness and rudeness of the vast population of that enormous and varied city. The sax touches and the film-noir story-telling is captivating- yet still, confection, for better or worse.I guess the themes being explored allow different interpretations- for me, the overall affect of the collection of tracks is that it seems like "pastiche", rather than coherent whole- in the sense of the "hodgepodge" definition of pastiche. And maybe that's Derek's point and his intention.In ConclusionIt's excellently done, catchy, filled with verve and variety, demonstrating fine musicianship from each participant in this production- progressive rock luminaries and newcomers too. AND at the same time, for better or worse, confectionary. I'm going with 3.5 candied stars, but rounding up to 4 thanks to the overall fine effort given.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — Cornwall's anachronistic Arthurian spacemen return with their seventh full-length studio album release since their formation (in Edinburgh) in 2010 and second in two years (which is unusually fast for them). 1. "Song of the Rainforest" (21:20) a vocal-less and more keyboard-generated epic than the usual Emerald Dawn offerings. Also, it feels as if the presence and contributions of Dave Greenaway and Tom Jackson here are on the same level of importance (and dynamics) as those of Ally and Tree. (36/40)- i. "Balance" - after a long 90-second intro of cave dripping sounds and two alternating sustained organ chords slowly establishing their pace and fullness and then the entrance and establishment of bass and drums into an awesome funk-lite vamp groove of two gorgeous Mellotron-like chords Ally enters with his seering electric guitar to deliver one of his best guitar solos ever--for five minutes! The contagious groove established by Dave Greenaway and Tom Jackson is awesome. - ii. Incursions - a stop-and-pause precedes a very slow switch to Smooth Reggae groove over which Ally solos with his tenor sax. As Trees synth strings enter (and Ally's tenor sax desists), the beat is sped up (we're now into the ninth minute), which prompts Ally to switch to his soprano sax--which gives Tree a little more room and license to embellish with her variety of synth strings riffs: often matching or meeting Ally's sax lines with her own.- iii. "Loss" - in the 11th minute another interlude of synth strings intervals paves the way for a heavier, almost ominous motif to set up with Tom's more tribalistic tom-tom-centered (synthetic talking drum?) drumming and Dave's heavily-wowed bass play being stomped over by some deep monster-saw keyboard and guitar riffs. The keyboards continue riffing--kind of soloing--for a couple of minutes over this motif before . . . - iv. "Regret" - the 14th minute has the establishment of a peaceful, perhaps sad motif of jungle/tropical sounds (including Tree's Amazonian flute) woven loosely around one another until the 18th minute when saw synth chords take over and Ally returns to shredding emotionally on his guitar. One of the most evocative, sensitive, and surprisingly tight--even thoughtful--sections of any Emerald Dawn song I've ever encountered. 2. "Rivers of Tears" (14:58) opens with a jaunty journey of jazz-classical-sounding solo piano play. Among the most impressive and pretty keyboard play I've ever heard from Tree! At 1:40 bass, drums, and, eventually, Ally's "reverberated-into-the-background" electric guitar slowly enter. Tree continues to tinkle the ivories within and behind the guitar, bass, and drums while adding some washes of synth strings to the mix as Ally continues shredding (as he does). Then Ally stops, making room for Tree to expand her piano note play as Tom and Dave slowly, gradually slow down and drop out. a pause/break at 3:30 results in the unleashing of Tree's reverb-drenched voice over only the banks of synth strings chords and still tinkling piano note play (mostly in progressing arpeggios)--which eventually becomes just synth strings as we enter into another little pause around 5:30. Here Tree establishes a chord progression with the repetition of four descending arpeggiated chords over which the rhythm section joins in and Ally deploys his tenor sax. Another pause at the seven-minute mark leads into a transference of the play of the descending chord pattern to synth strings as Tom and Dave kick back and Ally switches to electric guitar. Here Dave's bass playing is a bit rote and uninventive while the embellishments that Tom adds to his drumming feel a bit forced and "required" while Ally's guitar shredding sounds/feels . . . the same as ever. A little pause at the end of the tenth minute is filled with Tree's vocal lines until the band re-emerges with a kind of two-chord "tropical" vamp. Yet another stop and transition at 11:45 as the band shifts into a much more dark and ominous section--launched off as Tree shouts out a "Poison. Into. It's veins." declaration. This section could almost be coming from NIL or KING CRIMSON--even with Tree's operatic high-note repeat delivery of the word "poison." The motif then morphs in the second half of the 14th minute into something more akin to a Led Zeppelin descending chord progression--which it plays out to the song's end with embellishing accents coming from Ally's synths and Tom's drums. Not bad! (26.375/30)- i. "The Natural Cycle" - ii. "Disruption" 3. "Paradise" (8:56) opening with some excitingly pregnant synthesizer play--chords, bass, and peppy upper register riffs--which subside when Tree's plaintive, melancholy voice enters at 0:33 to introduce the song's theme. By the one minute mark she pauses wherein Tom and Mark enter with a cool, jazzy, STING "Englishman in New York"-like motif (which then happens to support Tree's "Englishman in New York" vocal melody lines). Nice bass line beneath Tree's organ chords as Ally enters with a bluesier Gilmour-like approach to his injections of guitar riffs and flurries. Around the four-minute mark the band slows things down, Tree's voice softens, while Mark and Tom's play kind of moves into greater prominence as Ally and Tree's keyboard play slides more into the background of the mix. Interesting! And I like it: I like having the bass and drums mixed in front of the keys, guitars, and saxes. The synth strings and guitar soloing in the next two minutes feel much more like the sound palette of Polish NeoProg masters COLLAGE's great textures on their Moonshine masterpiece (especially "The Blues"). In the seventh minute one of the keys begins to repeat and develop a melody line from THE MOODY BLUES' "Nights in White Satin," to which Tom backs down for a bit, but then everybody ramps up again into a fully-COLLAGE motif in which the synth strings continue soloing as other synth chords continue to deploy the "Nights in White Satin" chords and melody-reminders. Brilliant! And this is how they choose to end the song, the album! Awesome! Despite the "borrowing" of the sound palette and melody/chords, I finally feel as if The Emerald Dawn have arrived to the gates of top-tier prog, the symphonic side! (18.75/20)- i. "Losing Paradise"- ii. "Harmony Regained"Total Time 45:14I like the more sophisticated complexities ED are injecting into their compositions as it diminishes the dreaded monotony wrought of their old style of endlessly jamming over simple and often drawn-out single- and/or double-chorded vamps. Either their music theory has improved or they've decided to let go of the stoner-rock approach to song-rendering and employ more symphonic structuring for their music--whatever it is, I like it!A-/4.5 stars; a stunningly-improved advancement of compositional design yields the best album of The Emerald Dawn's career--one that has them knocking on the door of the Valhalla of the Symphonic Prog masters! I'm bumping up this rating into masterpiece status for the surprising display of growth as well as this being, in my opinion, Emerald Dawn's best album yet.

items.body: Review by VianaProghead — Review N� 982Le Orme is one of the longest lasting and best known Italian progressive rock bands. Le Orme was formed in Venice in 1966 by Aldo Tagliapietra (voice and guitars), Nino Smeraldi (guitars), Claudio Galietti (guitar and bass) and Marino Rebeschini (drums). Their first album, "Ad Gloriam" was released in 1968. From their psychedelic and beat initial roots, the band moved into much more increasingly sophisticated musical structures. In that line, the band released two excellent albums "Collage" in 1971 and "Uomo Di Pezza" in the following year. Their 1973 album "Felona E Sorona" is widely regarded as one of the top albums in the Italian progressive rock scene. By this time, the band consisted of Tagliapietra (mostly on bass with some guitar) along with keyboard player Tony Pagliuca and drummer Michi Dei Rossi."Felona E Sorona - Deluxe Edition (English And Italian Versions)" is a very special compilation album of Le Orme that was released in 2011. This is an economic package that includes their fourth studio album "Felona E Sorona", released in 1973, in its original Italian version, and their fifth studio album, which is the same album but in its English version and that was also released in the same year. This can be a very interesting compilation album because it includes the two versions of the album. As many of us know, "Felona E Sorona" is in general considered the best work from the band and is also considered a landmark to Italian progressive rock as one of the best and most important progressive rock albums ever made, especially in the Italian progressive rock scene. So, what we have really here is a great album in its two versions, probably at a cheaper price, and what will be a very worthwhile purchase, especially for those who are collectors and huge fans of Le Orme, fans of the Italian progressive rock or fans of the great prog music in general.As I'm going to review these two albums on Progarchives, in a more extensive way, I'm not going to do it at this moment. So, if you are interested to know, in more detail, what I'll write about them later, I invite you to read both of my reviews, in time. However, here I'm going to write something about them in a shorter way. So, of course, I'm not going to analyze them track by track, as I'm going to do, but I'm only going to make a global appreciation of both albums."Felona E Sorona" - Italian Version: "Felona E Sorona" is one of the classic albums of the Italian prog rock scene. The album quickly reached the top of the Italian charts giving the band their second gold record. Like many others, I find "Felona E Sorona" to be Le Orme's most fascinating work. In less than 35 minutes, Le Orme delivers probably their greatest masterpiece. Their high level of musicianship is evident over the all album. The focus is more on mood, song structure, and texture. As a concept work and despite the nine pieces, mostly short pieces and with a lot of variety, the album sounds very homogeneous and less like a collection of individual songs. This is an album that still has a strong influence in the world of progressive rock to the point that La Maschera Di Cera paid tribute to it by extending its theme and even going so far as to take up and transform the superb original cover. "Felona E Sorona" is a true classic of the movement and it's unforgivable not to have it if you like Italian prog rock. "Felona E Sorona" is an absolute must-buy."Felona E Sorona" - English Version: "Felona E Sorona" is a beautiful album, soaked with that 70's flavour that we all prog rock fans love. Although it's by no means technical, the band presents a unique sound that combines vocal parts that exude a unique sense of song with dramatic instrumental parts that make full use of synths and organs to portray a variety of scenes, including lyricism and thrills. It's an album of the golden years of progressive. Like their compatriots Premiata Forneria Marconi and Banco Del Mutuo Soccorso, "Felona E Sorona" was also released in the original Italian version and in the English version. At the request of Tony Stratton-Smith the owner of Charisma Records, Le Orme recorded an English version of the album with lyrics translated by Peter Hammill. It was also entitled "Felona E Sorona" and was also released in 1973. The English album is very similar, except that the vocals were more expressive and appropriate in Italian. This English version is also very good but listen to the Italian version because it's much better.Conclusion: Italian and English versions of the album give the listener the opportunity to hear the English lyrics, and yet enjoy the authentic feel of the original album. Well written notes in both Italian and English, including song lyrics. The essay in these notes gave me a proper understanding of what this album is about, as well as details about the album's production. As a bonus, there are also some band photos and copies of original mixes and vinyl stickers, both English and Italian. However, there's a poor sound quality for the English version. The volume is lower than that of the Italian version, which is a pity. Besides, I strongly prefer the Italian vocals to the English. I think escape to us some of the most important parts of the original album, which are the vocals. I can understand why many people, especially the non-Latin language speakers, prefer the English version. But, definitely, the original is always better than the copy.Prog is my Ferrari. Jem Godfrey (Frost*)

items.album: Event Review: Viljandi Folk Music Festival 2026 (Viljandi, Estonia; Thursday 23rd to Sunday 26th July 2026)
items.excerpt: It is Monday morning, checkout time at Grand Hotel Viljandi, and a German festival goer with his wristband still on hands back his room card and asks what a double costs. items.body: It is Monday morning, checkout time at Grand Hotel Viljandi, and a German festival goer with his wristband still on hands back his room card and asks what a double costs. Not for tonight, he specifies, for the same weekend next July, when Viljandi Folk comes round again, and preferably the very same room he has just spent four nights in. The receptionist explains that the system will not take a booking more than 11 months out. He takes this badly. He has plainly been turning it over for a while, perhaps since Thursday’s wild folk dances, perhaps during the downpour on Sunday night just before the grand finale, and now there is nothing to be done with the thought except carry it home.  That is a fairly standard state to leave Viljandi in. The town has something to do with it. Seventeen thousand people live on a ridge above a long glacial lake in southern Estonia, forest running down to the water on the far shore and the ruins of a 13th-century Livonian Order castle at the centre, the ground falling away in wide grass terraces cut by deep ravines. Those terraces are the festival: four outdoor stages sitting in the folds of the hills, Kaevumägi (Well Hill) at the top, the two Cherry Hills (Kirsimägi I & II) below it, and the Song Festival Grounds down on the flat. Two indoor rooms handle the rest: the Traditional Music Centre beside the ruins, the Ait or granary as locals call it, and the Sakala Centre in town, carrying the quieter programme by day and the wilder dances by night. Everything is ten minutes’ walk from everything else. To cross between Kaevumägi and the ruins you take the suspension bridge, 50 metres of it slung over a 13-metre trench and still swaying under everyone who steps on. Black sheep graze the slopes throughout, unbothered by any of it. And the festival is not only up on the ticketed grounds. It spills straight down into the old town, where two free stages run from lunchtime to eleven at night across all four days: the Green Stage on Laidoneri Square, where the dance schools set out workshops so anyone can learn the steps, and Sõprade Hoov on Lossi Street, a village-party yard open to any musician who fancies a turn. Seventy concerts happen out here, matching the paying stages exactly, strung along a street lined with a craft and design market where nobody checks a wristband. The programmed players are only half of it. Buskers of every age sprout across town, under gazebos and on pavements, some barely tall enough to hold the instrument, playing to whoever slows down. What carries across those slopes, alleyways and squares is pärimusmuusika, a word the English ‘folk’ flattens badly. For four days in late July this town does not commemorate its traditions so much as live inside them and shove them somewhere new. Most of what you hear sits on archival foundations: village fiddle tunes, bagpipe repertoire, regilaul runic song, the older Estonian and Finno-Ugric layers that were collected, catalogued and came within a generation of vanishing. Yet none of it is handled as museum material. This year’s theme, ‘To Each Their Own Instrument,’ was taken literally. Stages were packed with uncommon, traditional instruments most people couldn’t name, and within a day half of them were queuing to try one. Inside the Ait, the festival kept a second timetable. On three of the four nights, Thursday, Friday and Saturday, its great hall turned into Tantsumaja, the dance house, running from around 11pm until three or four in the morning while a rotating cast of folk musicians kept the tunes coming in relay. What happened on the floor was not a taught routine so much as a shared fluency: circles and couples moved through the room side by side, skill levels visibly ranging from a first attempt to real virtuosity, yet the general standard stayed remarkably high, dancers who had grown up on this repertoire picking out the shape of a tune they had never heard before and finding the steps inside it before the first verse was out. It all began, as it always does, with the parade winding through town on the Thursday early afternoon, before mayor Jaak Pihlak handed the ceremonial key to festival chief Ando Kiviberg, who has run this since its first edition in 1993. Just over 7,000 people came through the gates across that afternoon and evening, more day-one pass buyers than last year. In the Ait, six students turned the theme into a play, To Each Their Own Instrument, staged by director Lee Taul with a cast drawn from the Viljandi Culture Academy, the Estonian Academy of Music and Theatre and Tartu’s Eller college. Bagpipe, kannel and Teppo-type accordion were carried through the story by players still young enough to be studying them, the archive walking and talking rather than sitting in a case. The same idea took physical form a few streets over, on Pikk Street beside St John’s Church, where Pilliküla opened to the public for the first time: an ‘instrument village’ of close to 80 free workshops where anyone could sit down with a teacher and coax a first note out of a kannel, a bagpipe, a jaw harp, a fiddle, a talharpa or an accordion. “Musical heritage lives on as long as playing an instrument is common enough among the people,” Kiviberg said of the idea behind Pilliküla, the point being that a tradition survives by being played, not preserved. You could see the results all over town that weekend. Children busked on the hills and street corners with whatever they could play, one girl of maybe twelve and her violin set up between two stages with her case open for coins, taking more by evening than some of the market stalls. Up on the stages, the theme got loud. On II Kirsimägi that first afternoon, Gangar dug century-old dance tunes out of Norway’s national archives and ran them through a rock band. The Oslo five-piece build off springar and gangar rhythms, the old triple-time and walking dances they take their name from, Hardanger fiddle ringing over a rhythm section that a rhythm section hammering underneath, and drive the lot flat out. They played here in 2022, so they knew the crowd would dance, and it did. Down on the Song Festival Grounds, the sounds pulled from much further away. The Zawose Queens held the first Tanzanian booking in Viljandi’s history, and the sky opened just as they were due on, the kind of delay that empties a field. It did not. People pulled up hoods and waited, and by the time Pendo Zawose and her niece Leah came on, the wait had sharpened the air: Wagogo polyphony over ilimba thumb pianos and chizeze fiddle, a London rhythm section laying psychedelic rock beneath, a rain-soaked crowd that had chosen to be there. Their grandfather Hukwe Zawose carried this music around the world but never once let the women of his family sing lead; two generations on, his daughter and granddaughter stood at the front of the stage. The rain never really let up on the first evening, and neither did the appetite for dancing in it. Manhu closed Kaevumägi from half nine, five Sani players from the farming villages of the Stone Forest of Yunnan, together since 2003. They build from the lusheng, a bamboo mouth-organ whose drone sets the whole thing running, then stack the three-string adiza and call-and-response singing on top, with bass and drum kit worked so far underneath that the village music always keeps the upper hand. This is the sound of Sani daily life, drinking songs, welcome songs, love songs, seasonal tunes, nearly all of it built to move to, and they run a set the same way: a tune, a stop to walk the crowd through the steps, then the tune again, faster. Not a full sentence of English passed between the five of them and none was needed. One lifted a single leaf to his lips and bent a melody out of it; the steps were called by demonstration, arms up, follow this. By the last stretch a cold, soaked Estonian crowd that had never heard Sani music in its life was strung across the grass doing Yunnan courtship dances in the rain. Outdoors, the weather could be worn like a badge. Indoors, it exposed the festival’s one real weakness. Early shows had already packed the Ait to the walls. Over at the Sakala Centre, TõnisMägi, whose “Koit” became an anthem of the 1988 Singing Revolution, sold out fast enough to leave a queue stranded at a closed door, though these days the noise around him owes as much to his divisive public stances as to his songs. It happened repeatedly over the next three days: too many people, too few seats, and indoor rooms never built for crowds this size. Friday opened, in the early afternoon, on Ruhnu, with music and tales that had come closer than most to disappearing for good. Sounds and Stories from Ruhnu Island takes its name from a speck in the Gulf of Riga, Runö in Swedish, that held a few hundred ethnic Swedes and their own fiddle tradition until 1944, when the Soviet advance emptied the island almost overnight and left the repertoire alive only on tape. Fiddlers Karoliina Kreintaal and Lee Taul, with storyteller Kairi Leivo, have spent years playing it back off those recordings, and here they did it as a one-off. Ruhnu-born storyteller Jüri Keskpaik told the island’s life from the inside, its weddings, feasts, church and sea, while three members of the Nordic supergroup Groupa sat in: fiddler Mats Edén, flautist Jonas Simonson, and Terje Isungset, the Norwegian percussionist who builds his instruments from wood, stone and ice, all three back on Kaevumägi a few hours later for Groupa‘s own set. Behind them the whole time ran the island itself, archive film of Ruhnu’s shoreline, its people, customs and dances, a vanished community moving on screen while its own tunes played live underneath. Later that afternoon Mari Kalkun, born and raised in the Võru country of Estonia’s south-east and one of the few keeping its endangered Võro language sung, brought her kannel up against the kokle of Latvian player Laima Jansone. The kannel and the kokle are cousins, box zithers grown from the same ancient Baltic instrument and drifted so far apart that their traditions barely recognise one another now. Set them back together and that separation is nowhere to be heard: Kalkun’s playing drifting and psychedelic, her voice carrying the Võro songs she has spent a career prising out of the archive, against Jansone’s harder, more rhythmic attack, the two instruments circling, answering, now and then locking into a single line as though they had never parted. Then Kalkun left the stage entirely, microphone in hand, and walked into the middle of the field to sing from there, the crowd falling quiet and closing around her as she moved. In the evening, Amaro Duho kept their tradition in the family, literally. Matild Dobi assembled the band in 2021 from her own children, four decades after she helped start Ando Drom, one of the great names in Hungarian Roma music, and the point was to hold the songs together rather than let them scatter. It showed. Oláh Roma tradition on guitar, tambura and accordion, their own tunes threaded through the inherited ones, all of it played with the loose, unforced ease of people who do this around a table at home and happened, that night, to be doing it in front of a few thousand strangers. Estonian tradition can be handled far less gently, and Mandoterror proved it: a distorted rhythm section and a mandolin screaming where a lead guitar should be, five players who take Estonian folk melody and hit it at Nordic-metal weight. Kristjan Kuusmik stood out front on vocals, Tanel Sakrits‘ mandolin carrying the tunes a fiddle would usually hold, the old material cranked through songs from last year’s Nõiajaht and the anthem ‘Oru Leeni’. There is no compromise in it. The melodies land as though they were originally written for the extra volume: fast, sharp, and carrying clean across the grounds. The bigger stages found their real heat once it got dark, starting with Zetod on the Song Festival Grounds, the set that, by the reckoning of more or less everyone there, was where the festival properly began. Formed in Värska in 2003, they take Seto leelo, the old polyphonic singing of Estonia’s south-eastern border country, and play it at the speed and volume of a punk band: short hard songs stacked back to back, every word in Seto dialect, the pit moving from the first number and a whole field firing the lines back. In keeping with the year’s theme they built the set around four fiddles, one apiece, over accordion, bass and drums, the old dance tunes and archive material driven hard and fast. The singing that once went slow and unaccompanied, one voice leading and the rest answering, comes out here distorted and double-time, and nobody down the front drops a syllable. Most of the pull is frontman Jalmar Vabarna, who has fronted the band since they were teenagers and, off the stage, happens to be the elected ülemsootska, earthly stand-in for the Seto king. Same job either way, really, carrying his own corner of the country in front of as many people as will have it. By Saturday the site was full, 11,000 through the gates and the biggest crowd of the four days, the paths between stages packed from early afternoon as people wove from one set to the next. It all spilled onto the Song Festival Grounds, where HrayBery had the whole arena linking hands. The Polish-Ukrainian band rebuild village dance music from old scores and field recordings of the San river valley, a border region of eastern Galicia once shared by Poles, Ukrainians, Jews and Roma before post-war deportations scattered its people. They looked the part, in the Sunday best of a century ago: straw boater hats over dark suits and waistcoats for the men, high-collared white blouses and pale skirts for the women. Two fiddles, hammered dulcimer and frame drum drove the kolomyjkas, mazurkas, polkas and kozaks, and the crowd read the cue: great circling chains across the concrete, ring inside ring, while the grass banks behind filled with people watching them turn. A couple of hours later, still on the Grounds, the picture shrank from a full folk band to two women over a single instrument. Duo Ruut are Ann-Lisett Rebane and Katariina Kivi, who sit facing each other across one kannel, close enough to touch, one plucking while the other bows or drums the body, their voices soaring into harmonies that can hold a field still. Here they broke that on purpose, billing the set as Duo Ruut³ and pulling in Indrek Mällo on bass, Jaan Jaago on electric guitar, and on percussion Tõnu Tubli, who drummed a decade in Trad.Attack! and had already remixed the duo’s tunes on his own record. Outdoors, the expanded setup carried and got people moving, but it cost something too: the fine, quiet tension of two players negotiating one instrument is what makes them extraordinary, and a rhythm section inevitably paints over it. Still, once a real beat was locked under the runo song, the Grounds went from hushed to dancing. Over on II Kirsimägi, the boundary between the stage and the dirt dissolved entirely. Orkesta Mendoza opened with ‘Cumbia Volcadora’, six of them in matching suits, though nothing stayed buttoned down for long. Sergio Mendoza ran the set from the keys with an accordion slung across his chest, and on his shout of “¡Derecha! ¡Izquierda!” the whole field threw its hands right, then left, in time with him. Quetzal Guerrero sawed at the violin like an acrobat, Ozzy Acosta’s percussion kept the cumbia turning underneath, and Victor Hugo drove the band from the kit. Mendoza grew up in Ambos Nogales, the town the US-Mexico border splits in two, and the Orkesta plays what that town might sound like with the line gone: mambo, cumbia and ranchera rammed into surf guitar, psychedelia and indie rock. The Grounds kept filling as night came on, until the weekend’s largest crowd, some 8,000—packed in for Puuluup. Ramo Teder and Marko Veisson play the talharpa, a bowed lyre all but extinct outside the island of Vormsi, except they drum, bow, pluck, and brush it, feeding horsehair through loopers until a knocking, creaking rhythm rises out of a single ancient instrument. For a few numbers they brought out company: Tubli was back behind a kit, slamming real drums into a stage the pair usually run on loops and horsehair alone. In tuxedos and flat deadpan, Veisson’s voice rumbling low beneath Teder’s higher line, they sang in Estonian and a language of their own invention, stopping dead between numbers to sell the crowd straight-faced nonsense about what they’d just played. It was Veisson’s 50th, and when the field found out, thousands sang him happy birthday. He answered the only way that suited the night: throwing himself off the front to crowd-surf the field. They tried out new dance routines on the spot, saving their wildest choreography for a set that felt looser and warmer than usual. By the end, Duo Ruut were up there too: Rebane and Kivi crowding the microphones alongside Teder, Veisson, and Tubli, all five packed around the stand to see it out. Puuluup had warmed the field. OOPUS came to pound it. Mari Meentalo fed bagpipe, jaw harp and regilaul into a looper and handed the loops to Johannes Ahun’s analogue Roland synths, thousand-year-old runic song coming back out of the machines as acid house, while Aleksander Sprohgis’ lights, pinned to the beat, cracked across II Kirsimägi every time the bassline turned over and Raho Aadla danced it out at the front of the stage. OOPUS bill themselves as folk on acid and mean it to the letter: the bagpipe drone sat under a squelching acid line as though it had been waiting a millennium for exactly that, with their latest Reivlender playing as one long build. By mid-set a crowd that had spent the day watching thumb pianos and kannels was going properly, sweatily off, the oldest material on the whole bill turned into the closest thing Viljandi had to a nightclub. After midnight the festival split its mood in two. Kaevumägi turned inward for Kuula Hetke, the flute duo of Kärt Pihlap and Katariina Tirmaste, whose name translates as “listen to the moment” and whose method lives up to it: they take melodies from the home regions of their great-grandparents, Mulgimaa and Võrumaa, thread their own writing through them, and pull the whole thing apart and back together on stage. Two flutes, voice and electronics built into slow, elemental soundscapes, and beside them the visual artist Okeiko painted a video world in real time, improvising brushstrokes to match every shift in the music. The Song Festival Grounds went the other way, loud and communal, as Tuulebant+ marked ten years with a birthday set. What began as a handful of young Estonian lads deciding to play together has become a fixture of the dance floors, acoustic guitar, fiddle, bass and lõõts (the Estonian button accordion) under four voices, driving the kind of brisk, folk-rooted dance music that owes a clear debt to Untsakad and the Kukerpillid before them. For the anniversary they swelled the core band out with guests borrowed from other line-ups across the weekend, the plus in the name doing real work, and sent the last of the night’s crowd home dancing. Sunday came in warm and dry and ended wringing wet. The early afternoon on I Kirsimägi got a soft landing from Tell Your Birds, an Estonian, Latvian and Italian quartet who assemble their music from old tapes and Baltic tunes, running Estonian and Latvian folk melodies and field-recorded voices through electronics into long, drifting drones. Fiddle, bowed lyre and balafon carried the tunes up front while the fourth of them worked synths and effects beneath, turning a grey start into something to wake up slowly to.  By late afternoon, the sun had pulled the crowd onto Kaevumägi for Nancy Vieira, who brought Cape Verde to Viljandi, and morna to the festival for the first time in its history. Widely seen as the heir to Cesária Évora, Vieira carries that same slow, aching island sound. Born in Guinea-Bissau to Cape Verdean parents before moving to Lisbon at 14, she embodies the exact displacement morna is written about: the voice of the person who left. Backed only by guitar, cavaquinho, light percussion, and her own cool, unhurried lead, her set folded fado, Brazilian rhythms, and West African lines into songs from her 2024 album Gente. Then came the shift: for the final numbers, she invited the crowd right up onto the stage, turning the show into a full-tilt dance through the fast, bouncing tunes of Ano Nobo. The set the weekend had quietly been saving arrived that evening, and it went to Amy Laurenson. She had barely made the festival at all, held up by flight delays, cancellations, and baggage mishandling alongside guitarist Miguel Girão, reaching Viljandi just minutes before their Saturday slot on Kaevumägi in the rain and wind. Sunday finally did her justice, placing her at a grand piano inside the Ait. There, the Shetland pianist takes fiddle tunes written for a bow and hands them to the keys as a lead voice rather than accompaniment: reels arriving with their drive intact and their phrasing completely rethought. Out of the weather, the room went dead silent and stayed that way. It was the finest hour of the four days. Fittingly, the last word went to a band from the festival’s own backyard. Angus formed in 2010 out of Viljandi and its Culture Academy, and have spent the sixteen years since turning out a warm, unhurried reggae, ska and dub sung in Estonian, their 2023 record Vibratsioon hailed by Raadio 2 as the flagship of Estonian reggae-rock. Seven of them shut the festival down from the Song Festival Grounds, joined by guest vocalist Sofia-Liis Liiv, playing out into a downpour to a soaked crowd that skanked through the mud and bouncing along to thick dub basslines and hip-hop rhymes. Before the final fade, frontman Anton Ventsel signed the weekend off with a line worth keeping: “Have a good evening, a safe journey home, and folk is forever.” A local band, on the last stage, in the wet, closing a festival their own town has built its name on. Viljandi did not have its biggest year, but it had a better one than that. The man at the hotel desk had the right instinct and the wrong month. The next edition runs 22nd to 25th July 2027, worth writing down now, because he was not wrong about the room either.   The Viljandi Folk Music Festival returns in 2027, running 22nd to 25th July Ticket sales open in December, but keep an eye out HERE   [See image gallery at rhythmpassport.com] The post Event Review: Viljandi Folk Music Festival 2026 (Viljandi, Estonia; Thursday 23rd to Sunday 26th July 2026) appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

items.body: Dutch post-punk project Bragolin has cast a looming shadow across the international darkwave scene. For the past eight years, its music has passed from listener to listener through word of mouth and digital playlists assembled with the care once given to hand-dubbed mixtapes. With about 300,000 monthly Spotify listeners, the band now stands among the Netherlands’ most-listened-to contemporary wave exports, drawing an audience far beyond Utrecht. The band began there in 2013, when Edwin van der Velde transferred a guitar riff intended for his Dutch-language project Zwarte Poëzie onto a newly purchased Bass VI. The instrument changed the riff’s character and, with it, the course of his work. That piece became Into Those Woods, the first Bragolin song and a centerpiece of the 2018 debut, I Saw Nothing Good So I Left. The album has since been repressed six times on vinyl, while the track’s baritone hook carried it beyond ten million streams and onto darkwave dance floors around the world. Van der Velde expanded Bragolin in 2019 through Let Out The Noise Inside, a full-album collaboration with Adam Tristar that brought more electronic production into the project. Synth player Edwin Daatselaar joined the following year, establishing the current live duo; both musicians also play in Zwarte Poëzie. Bragolin has since performed more than one hundred shows across Europe and Latin America, including appearances at Wave-Gotik-Treffen, Amphi Festival, Cold Hearted Festival, Extramuralhas, and Kalabalik. The debut has continued to find new listeners as well: seven years after its release, This Grotesque Dance took off on TikTok and is now Bragolin’s most-streamed song, with over 7 million streams on Spotify alone. Bragolin’s third album, I Don’t Like What It Does to Me, retains the Bass VI, organ tones, and dance rhythms at the center of van der Velde’s writing while widening the arrangements with waterphone, synthetic ocean textures, seagull field recordings, strings, and a guitarless piece assembled entirely from layered Clavinets. “Visuals are what draw my attention,” van der Velde says, and references to The Lighthouse, It Follows, The Thing, and Invasion of the Body Snatchers enter these songs as stories of pursuit, artificial replication, surrender, and disappearance. Carrellee joins him on the album’s duet, Feel This Flame Unfold, extending a collaboration that will continue throughout the upcoming North American and European tours. Post-Punk.com spoke with van der Velde about the Nirvana and Björk records that first drew him toward songwriting, growing up beyond Drenthe’s blues and metal scenes, the growth of the Dutch wave underground, and Grauzone’s international role. He also discusses the unlikely longevity of Bragolin’s earliest songs, the backlash surrounding the video for Not All Are Real, the visual rules that keep faces concealed, the band’s first North American tour, and his ambition to develop concept albums and, perhaps one day, a Bragolin film. Bragolin. Photo by Lisanne Lentink Edwin, what were the first records or artists that seized your imagination growing up, and when did listening turn into the desire to write and perform your own music? When I was a kid, I mostly listened to local radio before I got a few pop music cassettes in the early ’90s, which were full of Eurodance. I didn’t care much about music until I discovered alternative music in my mid-teens. Nirvana and Björk were the artists who opened up that world for me. I was fascinated by what felt like the purity of Nirvana’s music, while Björk showed me how unconventional and unique an artist could be. Nevermind, Unplugged, and Post were the first three albums I owned. For most of those later teenage years, I listened almost exclusively to Nirvana. That inspired me to buy a guitar and start writing songs. You can still hear Nirvana’s influence beneath the surface in my music, in the song structures, the desire to write catchy melodies, and even in the way I often add the lyrics later in the songwriting process. Which books and writers had the strongest effect on you during those formative years? Were there particular novels that shaped Bragolin’s fascination with isolation, dread, and the uncanny? I’ve never been much of a reader. I have difficulty focusing on black letters on a white page. Visuals are what draw my attention. While I’m trying to translate the words into images, my mind often drifts off into its own story. I suddenly realize I’m no longer reading the text and have to go back and start again. It’s rare that I truly enjoy reading. So films have had a much bigger influence on me. It’s a shame, because all my life I’ve heard people say that books are so much more interesting than the films. Bragolin’s music and videos seem to draw from post-apocalyptic and horror cinema, including Gothic and folk horror, science-fiction paranoia, body horror, and cosmic horror. Which films first opened those worlds to you, and what do you tend to take from them—the setting, pacing, imagery, or emotional psychology? As a teenager, I was a big fan of the Terminator and Predator films. My dad has always loved action movies, so I grew up watching a lot of the classics with him. Later on, I discovered arthouse cinema, which gradually introduced me to folk horror. The Village (2004) and The Witch (2015) are great examples of the kind of settings and atmosphere I enjoy. I’m especially drawn to the vulnerability of the main character and the mystery and ambiguity of whatever they’re up against. I like to focus on that tension in my lyrics instead of the gore, although I enjoy those films as well. How did growing up in the Netherlands shape your musical imagination? Are there aspects of the Dutch landscape, culture, or temperament that have found their way into Bragolin? I don’t think growing up in the Netherlands consciously shaped Bragolin very much. I grew up in the province of Drenthe, where blues and metal were pretty much the only music scenes around. That made me realize quite early on that I had to look elsewhere to find like-minded people. Having said that, Dutch folklore is something I’d love to explore one day. I think it could make a great concept album. How would you describe the Dutch post-punk and darkwave scene today? Does it possess a character distinct from the scenes you have encountered elsewhere in Europe and Latin America? The Dutch wave scene has improved enormously over the last decade. It’s still a smaller and somewhat more reserved scene compared to our neighbouring countries, but it’s definitely moving in the right direction. Thanks to the hard work of promoters, musicians, and a new generation of fans, the scene has become much more hopeful than it was ten years ago. With festivals like Grauzone, Wavefest, and Momentum, we now have events of a high international standard. Artists like Adam Tristar, Raderkraft, Lifeless Past, De Ambassade, Silent Runners, Camy Huot, Pol, and many more are finding international success. A decade ago, the Dutch wave scene was mostly known internationally because Clan of Xymox came from here. Now there’s a much broader and healthier scene. Bragolin performed at Grauzone in The Hague earlier this year. What was that experience like, and what role has Grauzone played in connecting the Dutch underground with the wider international post-punk community? This year marked our second appearance at Grauzone. We were only announced as a last-minute replacement three days before the festival, so it was great to see such an enthusiastic response from the audience. What I enjoy most about Grauzone is seeing people from both the Dutch and international wave scene together, alongside visitors from outside the scene. Grauzone has made the genre much more accessible to people who might never have considered going to a post-punk or darkwave festival before. I think that’s played a huge role in helping the scene grow in the Netherlands and in connecting the Dutch underground with the wider international community. Can you take us back to the creation of “Into Those Woods”? Which arrived first: the baritone melody, the repeating organ hook, the rhythm, or those images of the manor, the swing, and the mysterious book? This is an interesting question because it was actually the very first Bragolin song I wrote. It all started with that guitar riff I originally had in mind for my other project, Zwarte Poëzie, in early 2013. In mid-2013, I bought a Bass VI, and when I tried the riff on that instrument, everything suddenly clicked. That Bass VI sound became the foundation of Bragolin when I decided to start it as a second project later that year. Because most of Zwarte Poëzie’s lyrics had been about my personal life, I wanted Bragolin to explore different themes. After watching The Evil Dead, I wrote the lyrics inspired by the film. Around that time I was also a big fan of the band The Organ and wanted to use an organ sound instead of relying mainly on synths like many darkwave bands. That became another defining element of Bragolin’s sound. “Into Those Woods” has surpassed fourteen million streams and become a modern darkwave classic. When did you first realize the song had taken on a life beyond the debut album, and how has your relationship with it changed since 2018? I started Bragolin without any expectations. We were just focused on making music the way we wanted to and making it as good as possible. Being in Zwarte Poëzie for eight years had taught me that success was difficult to achieve, although we did have some success with De Laatste Dagen as a minor dancefloor hit while I was working on the first Bragolin album. I assumed “Into Those Woods” might be too catchy and sound too clean for the goth scene, but fortunately I was wrong. The interesting thing is that the song’s reach kept growing year after year. Every year it felt like, “Okay, we’ve probably reached the ceiling now,” but it kept growing. What’s even more surprising is that “This Grotesque Dance” suddenly became a TikTok hit this winter, despite already being out there for seven years. Over the past year, it even surpassed “Into Those Woods” as our most streamed song. I’m very happy that our fans have embraced the new album just as much, and that Bragolin has grown beyond that one song. When we play live, it sometimes feels like we’ve already had a great show and then there’s that moment of, “Oh wait, we still have this song to come.” When you begin writing a Bragolin song now, what form does the first idea usually take? Could you walk us through the process of developing that fragment into a finished arrangement? For me, having a strong hook on top of a danceable beat and bassline is the foundation. I usually put on a drumbeat and play my Bass VI for hours until I find a riff that I like. I then record it and put it aside for weeks or even months. Listening back to a collection of these basic ideas later makes it easier to distinguish which ones have the most potential. After choosing the strongest one, I develop the riff into a song, often starting by humming vocal lines and eventually replacing those with rough lyrics. I then develop those lyrics into a story, which can be inspired by films I’ve recently watched. After that, I layer the song with additional instruments and sound recordings. On the latest album, I put more focus on that layering process than on the first two albums. For the next album, I would like to focus more on having strong foundations again, similar to the approach I took on the first album. “I Run and Hide” sounds heavily guitar-driven, yet its entire instrumental body was constructed from layered Clavinets. How did you record and process those layers, and what did that self-imposed limitation allow you to discover? After the second album, I bought a bunch of new instruments to embrace creativity. One of them was a small electric piano with different sounds built into it. For this song, I ran it through my Bass VI setup, which is why it doesn’t sound too far removed from the way the Bass VI normally sounds. Because it was a piano sound, I wanted to arrange it as if it could actually be played as a piano piece, with a low bass melody and multiple high melodies. I wanted it to feel like one instrument was playing the whole piece. It showed me that by limiting myself to one sound, I could still create a full arrangement with its own character. I Don’t Like What It Does to Me also incorporates field recordings, synthetic ocean textures, waterphones, and other unconventional sources. Could you identify a few moments where those sounds appear and explain how you manipulated them? For this album, I wanted it to have a more cinematic feel. One of the instruments I started using was the waterphone, which is often used in film scores and sound effects. It appears at various moments throughout the album, but it is especially noticeable at the beginning of the title track and This Presence Like a Breeze. This cinematic approach is also why I used a string section at the beginning of “Not All Are Real” to somewhat recreate the feeling of the opening of The Thing (2011), which is a prequel to the classic 1982 film. There are also two songs with ocean-inspired sounds: “Tar With Salt Foam” and “I Salute You Ancient Ocean”. For both songs, I created the sound of ocean waves with my Korg MS-20 by using synthesis rather than recordings of actual waves, while the seagulls were recorded as field recordings. I then processed and layered these sounds into the arrangements to create the atmosphere I was looking for. Where do your lyrics usually begin—with a personal experience, an image, a line from a book, or a scene from a film? How do you turn an outside reference into something that carries your own emotional meaning? It usually starts with a hummed vocal line, and then I look for words that fit the sounds and rhythm of that melody. From there, a few words become the basis of the lyrics. While watching films, I write down how I experience them visually and emotionally from the perspective of the protagonist. But I don’t want to create a direct interpretation of the film. It is more a starting point for my own lyrics, and often I turn it into my own story rather than sticking to the original inspiration. Which artists working in the current post-punk, darkwave, or experimental underground are exciting you most at the moment? Are there any Dutch acts in particular that you believe deserve a much wider audience? My listening has always been broader than just post-punk and darkwave, but from time to time I return to these genres, and there are still artists within the scene that I find very inspiring. I was pleasantly surprised by Carrellee’s music when she joined our record label, Young & Cold Records, with her self-titled 2025 album. I ended up listening to that album on repeat, which led to us getting in contact, collaborating on songs, and working together on upcoming tours. Other artists within our genre that I’ve been enjoying lately are Grundeis, The Woken Trees, The Soft Moon, Boy Harsher, Dead Man’s Bones, and Murder by Death. However, I have mainly been listening to a lot of 60s music, from Ennio Morricone and The Shadows to Nancy Sinatra and Roy Orbison. It is still often dark and melancholic music, and I think I know what elements to take from other genres and what to leave behind when creating my own music. Bragolin’s videos have become an important extension of the songs, from the manor and woodland imagery of “Into Those Woods” to the nocturnal pursuit through streets and cornfields in “I Run and Hide.” How closely involved are you in developing those concepts, and what do you look for in a director? I usually create at least one music video per album myself. For the others, when looking for a director or editor, the most important thing is that they understand the music, respect our visual identity, and have a fitting portfolio. With the new album, I wanted to create more original footage instead of reusing existing material as on previous albums. My role is mainly setting guidelines, such as avoiding showing faces clearly in our visual content. We call this anonymity. This connects with our album covers, which are all portraits shot from behind, and our lyrics, where we also leave room for interpretation rather than explaining everything too clearly. I Run and Hide was made by two very talented film students, Maria Gaedcke and Jonathan Eder. It was our first time working with a larger production. My idea was to combine the inspiration for the song, the film It Follows (2014), with the new album cover’s figure in the nightgown, while taking the opposite approach to the film by not showing the antagonist explicitly. The video for “Feel This Flame Unfold” was created by State of Poison, who had caught our attention with several great animated productions. Animation offered a chance to explore another style, and I’m really happy with how all the videos turned out. For “Not All Are Real,” you connected The Thing and Invasion of the Body Snatchers with contemporary anxiety about artificial replication, using intentionally unnatural AI-generated imagery. What creative and ethical boundaries did you establish for that video, and did the response to it alter your view of the technology? Even though it received quite a lot of negative responses, I still think the concept I wanted to create was only possible in this way. The video is about artificial replication, so using AI-generated imagery became part of the concept itself rather than just a production tool. Filming people in public without their consent would have raised ethical concerns. Emptying the streets of major cities around the world to create a film set and hiring hundreds of actors simply isn’t realistic within the budget of an independent band. Animation, on the other hand, wouldn’t have captured the unsettling feeling of cloned humans that I was looking for. The only real alternative would have been to abandon the concept and make a completely different video. I also found it interesting that we’d previously used existing footage in our videos, which raises ethical questions of its own, yet that never received the same criticism. That said, the reaction was enough for me to decide: never again. Bragolin will embark on its first North American tour this fall. What are you most looking forward to experiencing on this run, and when you look beyond it, where would you like to take Bragolin next—musically, visually, and geographically? We have had a following in North America for a long time, and the requests for us to come over have gone unanswered for many years. I’m mainly looking forward to finally meeting those fans who have been following us from the beginning and hopefully giving them the show they’ve been waiting for. Looking beyond this tour, I’d like Bragolin to remain a constant by continuing to make albums for many years to come. I’d also love to explore the possibility of creating concept albums, which is an element from the past I’d like to bring back to the present, and combine that with even more visual storytelling, perhaps one day creating our own dedicated film. Geographically, there are still plenty of places we haven’t visited. In early 2027, we’re planning a West Coast tour and a return to Latin America.§ Listen to I Don’t Like What It Does To Me below and order the album here. I Don’t Like What It Does To Me by Bragolin Looking towards the horizon, Edwin Van der Velde hopes to expand Bragolin through future concept albums and, eventually, a film devoted to the project’s visual world. Yet, the immediate priority is Bragolin’s first North American tour. Van der Velde and synth player Edwin Daatselaar will take the band on the road alongside Carrellee for the thirty-date North American Hope Tour, beginning September 3 at X-Ray Arcade in the Milwaukee area. Bragolin has maintained a substantial North American audience for years, yet these will be the duo’s first performances on the continent. The route continues through the Midwest, Ontario and Quebec, the Northeast, the South, and Texas before ending October 11 in Tulsa. Bragolin then returns to Europe for dates beginning October 31 in Utrecht and running through December 19 in Brussels, followed by São Paulo and Santiago in February 2027. A separate West Coast tour is also being planned for early 2027, though its dates have yet to be announced. The schedule reflects the unusual way Bragolin’s audience has grown. Into Those Woods accumulated listeners steadily until it passed ten million streams, while This Grotesque Dance found a new audience through TikTok seven years after its release and eventually became Bragolin’s most-streamed song. Those songs reached North America well before the band could follow them. After years of requests from listeners across the continent, van der Velde and Daatselaar will finally meet that audience in person this fall. items.body: Eye New Dark Adore self-released Eye New Dark is the solo project of Null Device’s Jill Sheridan, and while it shares that modern synthpop act’s lushness and melodic bent, departs from it in some interesting ways. Sheridan has always been a powerful vocalist with excellent control and feeling, and the major contrast in the material on Adore is in hearing her over some more bright and even brash sounding material. Single “Backwards Through That Door” features spritely synth arpegios and peppy drum programming, with Sheridan riding the beat, choosing her spots to move into her upper range for emphasis, the phrasing as important to the song’s feeling as any given sound design element. Similarly, when she sings on the rhumba-beat driven “Real Life”, its her clarity and measured performance that allows her to cut through the brushy percussion sounds, big pads and swelling bells, recalling some of OMD’s more baroque moments. Perhaps the most revelatory moment is closer “Eyes in the Dark”, a track that is musically designed around a sort of stop-start rhythmic movement, the spaces between each small burst of instrumentation smoothed by the lush and layered vocal recordings, filling the space without crowding it. It’s a lovely collection of tracks that shows off versatile takes modern and classic synthpop styles, driven by a genuinely skilled performance. Adore by Eye New Dark Circa Tapes Climbers LVLZ You’ll always be getting a slightly rejiggered formulation of the styles and influences which shape Adam Sieczka’s work as Circa Tapes every time you check in with it, and new EP Climbers is no exception in that regard. Traces of left-field pop and post-punk, along with some of the project’s longstanding interest in minimal wave can still be found in the corners of these four tracks, but it’s a dark and metallic approach to body music rhythms which holds sway (Ortrotasce might be the only other current American act pulling from the same corners, though the trajectories of the projects have been quite different). The metallic reverb which swirls above the snares of “Pulse Fate” might connote either vintage Underworld or possibly Sieczka’s previous work in Kill Memory Crash, while the smoky and dense waves of feedback chopped into “Stukka”‘s acidic EBM brings the underrated work of European experimentalists NTRSN to mind. Colour, funk, and a distinctly American sardonicism blur the jagged edges of Climbers‘ beats. Climbers by Circa Tapes The post Observer: Eye New Dark & Circa Tapes appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: Magic Wands released the single “Diamond Rain” on August 14, 2026 through Metropolis Records. The Los Angeles duo of vocalists and guitarists Dexy and Chris Valentine mix dream-pop with shoegaze, post-punk and goth, and the track is the first to be lifted from a new Magic Wands album due in early 2027. It is out digitally, with a self-made video posted to the band’s YouTube channel the same day. Diamond Rain by Magic Wands What Magic Wands say about ‘Diamond Rain’ The duo describe the song as deliberately open rather than fixed: “the song doesn’t have one fixed meaning. To us, it’s about moving toward the light, finding beauty after darkness and allowing people to discover their own meaning within it.” They made the accompanying video themselves and explain how the look was built: “using old cameras, lights and mirrors to create textures and effects that give it a dreamlike feeling.” “Diamond Rain” streams and downloads through Bandcamp and the usual digital services. No physical edition has been announced, and the duo have not named the 2027 album or given it a date. ‘Diamond Rain’ follows two EPs and a Peter Murphy remix The single closes an unusually busy eighteen months. The album “Cascades” arrived on October 24, 2025, trailed by the double single “Time To Dream” backed with “Armour (River Remix by Lost Signal)” the previous month. A Delerium remix of “Moonshadow” followed on March 13, 2026. Two EPs came after that. The “Wishing Well” EP, six songs issued on April 24, 2026, was preceded by its title track in February and by “Sacred Mirrors”, a January 2026 collaboration with John Ashton of The Psychedelic Furs. The six-track “Remixes” EP landed on June 12, 2026 and reworked material from “Cascades”. In between, the pair remixed Peter Murphy; Side-Line covered that single when Peter Murphy released “Swoon (Magic Wands Remix)” on May 29, 2026. About Magic Wands Magic Wands formed in Nashville in 2008 around Dexy and Chris Valentine, who share vocals and guitars, and later moved to Los Angeles. Metropolis Records describes their sound as heavily textured guitars, droning synths and ethereal vocals. The duo have released through Metropolis for over a decade. Side-Line first covered them in April 2022 around the single “Fortune”, then the single “Time” in May 2023 and the remix album and tour that August. The album “Switch” followed in 2023 and was reviewed here that September. “Cascades” came in October 2025 and drew the run of singles, remixes and EPs that “Diamond Rain” now brings to a close, with the next album set for early 2027.

items.body: ITCH have made a debut record called “House of Ghosts” available to stream on Escape.ai, a distribution platform and creator marketplace for generative AI and game-technology work founded by John Gaeta, an American visual effects designer, inventor, and creative director. The project describes the album like this: “House of Ghosts is a dark, alternative journey through memory, identity, loss, and the parts of ourselves that refuse to disappear. Split between ANIMUS and ANIMA, the album explores masculine and feminine inner worlds as two haunted sides of the same soul.” Ten tracks are posted with official audio and full lyrics: “Somewhere to Hide“, “Two”, “Temp”, “Throne”, “Alone”, “Time”, “Wrong”, “Son”, “Keep Your Roots” and “Void”. The lyrics deal with grief and absence (“Time takes everything”), sibling violence (“There were two. Then there was one”), suppressed anger (“It’s not anger, it’s a temperature”) and isolation (“I’m alone in my skin”). No writer, performer, producer or engineer is named against any of them. Due to the ban on AI music on several platforms, the album will probably only be available on Escape.ai for the moment being. About Escape.ai Escape.ai is a next-generation entertainment streaming and content distribution platform dedicated to pioneering the future of digital storytelling. Founded by Academy Award-winning visual effects designer John Gaeta (The Matrix), the platform serves as a curated, premium showcase for “Neo Cinema” and “Neo Play”. Unlike open social media feeds where AI content is frequently lost in the noise, Escape.ai positions itself as a prestige destination for premium, human-authored stories that are super-amplified by technology. The network champions independent creators, offering them a way to scale their original intellectual property and achieve blockbuster-level world-building without relying on traditional, rigid Hollywood studio pipelines. The network is actively streaming across major platforms like Roku and The Roku Channel, Amazon Fire TV, Samsung Smart TVs, and LG TVs, with expansion onto Apple TV and PC environments.

items.body: Elsieanne Caplette, singer and composer of Montreal trip-hop duo Elsiane, announced on August 12, 2026 that she has begun a solo project separate from the band. She made the announcement in a message to subscribers of the Elsiane Bandcamp page, and used the same message to confirm that Elsiane are planning tour dates for 2027. No title, release date, format or label has been named for the solo material. What Elsieanne Caplette has confirmed so far Caplette said she has been working on the project privately and is holding the details back for now: “Lately, I’ve been quietly working on something that’s entirely my own. I’m beginning a new solo chapter. I’m not quite ready to reveal everything yet, but I can tell you that this project feels deeply personal and unlike anything I’ve shared before.” She pointed readers to a new mailing list at elsieannecaplette.com for the first announcements. Nothing further about the solo work is public: no title, no release date, no format, no label, no collaborators and no production credits. Her bandmate Stephane Sotto is not mentioned in the message, and Caplette does not say whether the solo project affects Elsiane. Elsiane tour dates are planned for 2027 The message closed with the band’s own plans. Caplette wrote: “And for everyone wondering, yes… Elsiane is planning some tour dates next year and some surprises. We’ll be sharing more details this fall.” No cities, venues, countries or on-sale dates are confirmed, and the duo have not said whether the run supports new Elsiane material. The wording places the full announcement in autumn 2026. Elsiane have been signalling a return to the road for some time. Caplette told Canadian Beats in September 2023, ahead of the self-titled album, that the duo were “planning to have some shows for next year” and were hoping to book tour dates. Those dates did not follow, which makes the 2027 window the first firm timeframe the band have given since. The most recent Elsiane release is the self-titled album “Elsiane”, issued on October 3, 2023 through Labratoryband Inc. and produced by David Bottrill. Side-Line covered it when the duo prepped an October release for the all new album, simply titled “Elsiane”. Seven tracks: “Traces of the Heart”, “Tu Mirada”, “Sinai”, “Loneliness”, “Soul Travelling”, “Fading Star” and “Under Aghast”. Elsiane by E L S I A N E About Elsiane Elsieanne Caplette was born in Montmagny, Quebec, and trained in classical music at the Lima Conservatory in Peru; Wikipedia records that she grew up in Peru, sang in a group there and moved to Montreal in 1999. There she met Stephane Sotto, a self-taught drummer born in Montreal. The two began working together in 2000 and named the project by joining the first four letters of her first name to the last three of his. Their music pulls on jazz, downtempo, rock, classical, electronic and world music, and they cite the trip-hop of Massive Attack and Portishead alongside Bjork, Kate Bush and Peter Gabriel. The debut album “Hybrid” arrived on May 1, 2007 on Vega, with Nettwerk issuing it in the United States the following year. Live work followed, including tours with Delerium and Beast, and a contribution to the soundtrack for Quebec City’s 400th anniversary alongside Cirque du Soleil and Booka Shade. On stage the line-up has included Jeff Feldman on bass and keyboards and Philippe Look on guitar and keyboards. The self-produced second album “Mechanics of Emotion” followed on April 10, 2012 on Labratoryband Inc., trailed by the single and video “Underhelped”, and drew more openly on acoustic and traditional instruments. A third album, “Death of the Artist”, came out independently in 2017 after the duo ran into difficulties with the music industry, and in 2018 they worked with the writer Rich Shapero on “Rin, Tongue and Dorner”. Side-Line has tracked the band across that stretch, covering the 2016 surprise single “Unstable” and the 2020 return single “Sinai”. Sotto’s father died in 2018 and the pair started writing the next record in his memory, with production beginning in July 2019 under Bottrill. “Tu Mirada”, released in October 2022 and sung in Spanish, drew on Caplette’s Peruvian upbringing. The finished album added guest players including Pedro Eustache, Trey Gunn of King Crimson, Tony Grey and Caroline Plante, and came out on October 3, 2023. It remains the duo’s last release, and Caplette’s solo announcement is the first news from either member since.
